title: Planning the site with pi
agentLog: Reviewed the assignment requirements directly from the class slides (multi-page nav, animation, easter egg). Proposed a full plan: plain HTML/CSS/JS (no Astro), a minimal/clean visual style chosen after rendering 3 side-by-side mockups, an illustrative 36-flight network across all 6 continents for the home page animation, and an easter egg where clicking a plane reveals a persistent emissions trail plus a one-line aviation-emissions fact.
yourNotes:
1. I initially wanted to use Astro for this project since I hadn't used it before, but the agent recommended plain HTML+CSS for the use case I described. After seeing a pros/cons comparison, I decided to stick with that recommendation — it assured me that moving to Astro later, if needed, would not be a hassle.

2. A shared layout across all 4 pages made sense to me.

3. The easter egg took the longest to explain and finalize. I wanted something simple and assumed it understood what I meant (36 routes between the 6 continents), but the math didn't quite work out, and there was a series of iterations on which routes to keep vs. discard. In hindsight this wasn't a great use of tokens — it could have been a clarifying question back to me instead. For now, I stuck with a fixed list of pre-determined routes rather than fetching real ones from the web.

4. For the visual style, the two directions I liked most were minimalist/clean and retro. Seeing rendered PNG mockups of the map before committing to one made the decision much easier.

5. I think it would help to explicitly separate which parts of this are actual research decisions (needing more thought/options) from which parts are purely decorative (and could use less effort/resources). Using different agents for these two categories is one option, though I'm unsure how well they'd coordinate with each other.

6. This is the first time I've seen an agent take its own screenshots of the website to verify things were working — I found that genuinely interesting.

title: Built the full site in 5 staged commits
agentLog: Implemented the plan: data files (routes, facts, dev log), shared layout/nav, the 4 HTML pages, the animated map (36 routes, staggered reveal), and the easter egg (click-to-reveal trail + fact tooltip). Verified everything with real headless-browser tests, not just visual inspection — caught and fixed a bug where city-dots were blocking clicks on planes at shared destination cities. Committed in 5 logical stages matching the build order, then pushed and helped enable GitHub Pages.
yourNotes: Grouping commits by type of change helped make the chain of decisions much easier to follow.

title: Six refinements after trying the live site
agentLog: Changed the animation model from 36 simultaneous planes to a single aircraft that flies each route in sequence, using a proper airplane icon (verified its orientation empirically before wiring up rotation math). Slowed the flight speed (1.6s to 4.2s per leg). Route lines now fade out and are removed after landing, while emissions trails persist independently in a separate SVG layer. The fact tooltip now dismisses itself when a new one is triggered instead of stacking. Emissions particles now start small, dark, and concentrated at the flight path, then slowly grow and lighten as they spread outward over ~7 seconds. Restructured the dev log data/page into two columns.
yourNotes: It cost about $4 to try to get the plane animation looking good, upon which I steered the agent to revert to a simpler task and asked to abandon the more ambitious plans.

title: Created --reality-check skill
agentLog: Wrote a reusable skill that the agent loads when you ask for a 'reality check' on any idea or proposal. The skill ensures balanced tradeoff analysis by enforcing at least one genuine pro and one genuine con, both specific to your actual context. Committed to .pi/skills/reality-check/SKILL.md.
yourNotes: I used Haiku, since I expeced fewer queries for a simpler task. It wrote a pretty comprehensive skill.md, though it did not inittially follow the template in the class repo, and only told me it did not have access to it after I probed it to ask why the template was not followed. I liked that ti checked pi's skills template too inittially. I had initially interpreted the 'verification' aspect to be some sort of user feedback on the output of the skill, but let it be a simple check since I did not want it to get into an iterative loop with this one skill.
